title: Every Living Thing Meets Death and Passes Away
intro: Ibn Munadhir mourns his friend Abd al-Majid ibn Abd al-Wahhab al-Thaqafi, who al-Mubarrad says died at about twenty. Abu al-Faraj relates that the poet cared for his friend during a serious illness in Basra and that Abd al-Majid recovered and lived for a long time before a fatal fall from a roof. In a second account in the same book, al-Jammaz places the fall during a month of wedding feasts, as Abd al-Majid bent to retie a loose awning rope. The elegy moves from mountains worn away and kings betrayed by their fortresses to the young man whose bier the speaker follows. When the friend he calls can no longer answer, he bids his eyes begin weeping again.

translation: Every living thing will meet death and pass away.
No living creature, for all its hoping, can endure for ever.
1.sharh: The dead man is still unnamed. The opening gives every listener a place among those to whom the judgement applies, including the speaker who survives his friend.

translation: Death fears nothing and spares
no parent and no child.
2.sharh: Death owes no deference to one generation before taking the next. The pairing of parent and child prepares for a young man's death long before an old man's would have been expected.

translation: Time scores the peaks of Radwa
and brings the rocks of Habbud down.
3.sharh: Time wears a mark into one mountain and dislodges the stones of another. Two distinguishable features of the landscape make a universal assertion testable by the eye.

translation: The blows of events and the days leave
a fissure even in the great hard rock.
4.sharh: The rock's smooth hardness makes the weakness in it hard to imagine. A crack gives time a small beginning from which it can undo even that apparent permanence.

translation: God does as he wills and it comes to pass.
No one can turn back what God has done.
5.sharh: After describing change through its marks on stone, he speaks of it as divine action. The movement forward in “comes to pass” has no corresponding movement back.

translation: I see us as grain the days are harvesting,
some of it standing, some already cut.
6.sharh: The living and the dead belong to one crop. Being upright means the reaper has yet to reach that stalk, a temporary difference visible across the same field.

translation: We are like riders bound for death, pressing
swiftly towards a watering place all must reach.
7.sharh: A band of thirsty travellers drives eagerly towards water. Making death that destination lends the ordinary haste of travel a meaning its riders may never have intended.

translation: Where is the lord of the secure fortress at Sura,
the lord of the high, strong-built palace?
8.sharh: The building can still be described in detail while no answer comes from its lord. The turn to a fortified town introduces a case in which every ordinary precaution was available.

translation: He raised its pillars, fitted it with
two iron gates and ringed it round with troops.
9.sharh: The defence is built in layers, beginning at the pillars and ending with a living ring of soldiers. Counting the two iron gates prepares their reappearance after the ruler has fallen.

translation: Tribute came to him from the lands between Sana'a
and Egypt, as far as the villages of Bayrud.
10.sharh: Revenue draws a map of his authority from southern Arabia to Egypt and beyond. It all travels inwards to one ruler, concentrating the scale of his loss of power.

translation: Behind him you would see great bands of horses,
sweeping past with lions on their backs.
11.sharh: We first see the mass of animals, then the riders they carry. Lions on horseback lend the guard a second, imagined kind of strength.

translation: Time took aim at his very person and struck home
with a straight-flying arrow out of death's quiver.
12.sharh: A marksman can single out one figure in a crowd. The arrow of death does exactly that to the individual whom the army had made almost invisible.

translation: Then no fortress saved him from death,
with its ditch in front and its two iron gates.
13.sharh: The two gates are recognised from the earlier description. With the ruler dead they now stand as evidence of failure, alongside the ditch between him and an ordinary attacker.

translation: And kings before him peopled the earth,
aided by victory and support,
14.sharh: A single ruler gives way to a succession of kingdoms that filled the earth. Their access to powerful allies and victory extends the test beyond one unlucky defence.

translation: and many a mighty one bound his head with the crown,
fierce-eyed, guarding his people, with a countless following.
15.sharh: The crown is wound round a head like a band of cloth. Fierceness, loyalties and numbers complete the portrait of the kinds of excellence a king could call his own.

translation: Had the days ever made one man immortal
for nobility, they would have kept Abd al-Majid.
16.sharh: Only now does the private name enter the public meditation on death. The condition lets him declare his friend's worth while conceding that no worth could have saved him.

translation: On the day Abd al-Majid went away,
he brought down a pillar no one thought could fall.
17.sharh: The straight young figure has become a supporting pillar. Repetition of the verb for demolition makes the fall sound all the more extraordinary after the images of solid masonry.

translation: Neither his bier nor the men who bore him knew
what weight of goodness and generosity that bier carried.
18.sharh: A burden can be weighed without its value being known. He imagines the unknowing bier and its living bearers alike as instruments carrying more than a body.

translation: They buried in the earth good judgement and resolve,
the one match for an obstinate, contentious foe.
19.sharh: Qualities take the body's place in the sentence. Judgement and resolve go into the ground with someone who could hold his own against the most intractable opponent.

translation: Alas for the hands that scattered earth upon him, for the hands
that buried him, for what they hid in the ground.
20.sharh: The mourners break up into working hands. A few handfuls of soil can cover what the speaker regards as a whole treasury of human qualities.

translation: Abd al-Majid brought my pillar down. I used
to find strong shelter in that pillar of his.
21.sharh: The earlier pillar now has a personal owner. We learn what it upheld, the speaker's own ability to find his footing or take shelter in his friend.

translation: My soul almost poured away over him
when he lay bound in a bundle and wrapped in striped cloths.
22.sharh: His own soul seems ready to flow away. Of the friend who once moved and spoke, all he can see now is cloth wrapped and tied around a body.

translation: With Abd al-Majid went the lifeblood of my soul.
My fortunes stumbled after they had risen.
23.sharh: Blood deep inside the heart stands for the friend's value. The second image gives good fortune legs that once recovered their footing and have now stumbled under him.

translation: In losing Abd al-Majid I lost the use of my right hand,
and generosity lost the use of hers.
24.sharh: The poet feels the loss in the hand he used to act and give. Then generosity itself acquires a right hand, paralysed by the same loss.

translation: The water of youth gave him drink and he swayed
like a fresh and pliant bough.
25.sharh: Memory restores motion to the body last seen in its shroud. Youth waters the boy like a grower tending a shoot, and his supple movement answers the water.

translation: Eyes rose towards him, and no one
who wished to add a grace could add a thing.
26.sharh: People lift their eyes to look. The verse imagines an admirer with the power to improve what he sees and leaves him with nothing to do.

translation: Whenever I remember him, something catches
in my throat and along the great vein of my neck.
27.sharh: What begins as a memory shows itself as an obstruction in the throat. The jugular beside it brings the discomfort disquietingly close to the bloodstream.

translation: I seem to call him when he is close at hand,
even as I call him from a place far off.
28.sharh: Memory makes his friend almost adjacent. Calling exposes how far the dead have gone, so nearness and distance occupy the very same act of address.

translation: If he can no longer answer, once he was
all ears and gladness whenever he was called.
29.sharh: The silence of death is set alongside an exact social memory. Hearing a call, he used to turn willingly and with visible pleasure towards the caller.

translation: He was my protection until time swept him away.
What grief now for one left utterly alone.
30.sharh: The man who gave him shelter has himself fallen to the power he sheltered him from. Two words for being alone fill the space where a second person once stood.

translation: Young man who graced every assembly,
I do not see you where the people gather.
31.sharh: He looks for someone whose presence used to distinguish a public gathering. A crowd of witnesses makes the missing figure more conspicuous to the one who knew him.

translation: I have betrayed your love. I did not die of grief
after you. How hard I must be to bear your loss.
32.sharh: Survival becomes evidence for an accusation of disloyalty. The apparent compliment about toughness is bitterly directed against the man who has managed to live on.

translation: Yet I shall weep for you as long as old she-camels yearn
and a strong she-camel is urged on in hobbles.
33.sharh: Camel cries and the urging of mounts give his vow a duration extending through ordinary desert life. The yearning voice also gives the tears a sound to answer.

translation: If a living man could ransom a dead one, your life
would be bought with mine, with all I earned and all I inherited.
34.sharh: The offer spends the speaker himself before it spends his property. Newly acquired and inherited possessions complete the inventory of a ransom he knows no one can accept.

translation: Against my will you went ahead of me.
Against my will you were lowered into a side-niched grave.
35.sharh: He had no say in which friend went first and none in the lowering of the body. Identical expressions of unwillingness accompany two very different movements away from him.

translation: You were my safeguard, you were a sky
by which my earth came alive and my branch turned green.
36.sharh: The young man watered by youth now supplies rain to someone else. Speaker and friend become an entire landscape in which the loss of the sky means the loss of growth below it.

translation: You left the enemy nursing spite dumbfounded,
and returned a loyal friend's love twofold.
37.sharh: He could leave a man who secretly hated him speechless. A friend who showed him affection received twice as much in return.

translation: Abd al-Majid has become a calamity, who once
was our hope against the turns of a thankless age.
38.sharh: The boy was once the person one hoped would help in misfortune. His death is now the misfortune itself. The Arabic words for calamity and hope sound close as they exchange places.

translation: Just when his accomplishments had come to flower
and he had put on the fresh robe of youth.
39.sharh: His training and gifts had come to maturity just as youth itself was new. The fresh robe recalls the burial cloths, giving this memory of first putting it on a painful brevity.

translation: My sorrow that I do not see you, that you have
no answer for me if I call.
40.sharh: Two ways of recovering the boy fail in succession. He cannot be seen and his voice cannot be summoned, although the sentence still addresses him as someone present.

translation: Even if the anguish of mourning him has not killed me,
I shall go to the limit of my strength.
41.sharh: He takes up his earlier charge against himself for living. The energy remaining to a survivor can still be spent by mourning to the utmost of his powers.

translation: I will assemble mourners bright as the stars
of night, striking the smoothness of their cheeks,
42.sharh: A gathering of mourning women becomes a constellation before the focus moves in to their hands and cheeks. The assembly gives his solitary grief other bodies and voices.

translation: women in pain, weeping for a liver burning
over him and for a heartsick heart,
43.sharh: The liver is a conventional seat of passionate feeling in Arabic poetry. Its heat and the stricken heart give the women a bodily measure of the suffering they lament.

translation: and for an eye forever struck, to which
time has said, “Take no rest. Pour out your tears.”
44.sharh: An eye stung by an irritant keeps watering. Time has both inflicted the injury and given the eye its orders, so even a moment's rest would feel disobedient.

translation: Whenever weeping masters you and you empty
a full bucket for Abd al-Majid, begin again,
45.sharh: The eye is addressed as someone working at a well. A brimming bucket would seem a prodigious amount of tears, but emptying it only sets the rhythm for another.

translation: for a young man it is fitting to weep for,
a young man fit for the praise of odes.
46.sharh: The close pairs tears for the dead with the praise a living man merits. The poem has supplied both, so the right to mourn rests on a life whose particular worth the listener has now seen.

1.1.4.head: الحِمام
1.1.4.meaning: Death as a creature's appointed end.

1.1.5.head: مودٍ
1.1.5.meaning: Perishing or passing away. The recited half gives the participle a sustained final vowel.

2.1.3.head: المَنون
2.1.3.meaning: Death or the passage of time considered as cutting short a lifespan.

2.1.6.head: تَرعى
2.1.6.meaning: The beginning of tar'a, completed across the break. With the following preposition it means “spare or show regard for”.

3.1.1.head: قَدَحَ
3.1.1.meaning: Scores or eats away a hard surface, leaving a visible mark.

3.1.4.head: شُمروخ
3.1.4.meaning: Protruding mountain pinnacles or narrow high points.

3.1.5.meaning: Radwa, a mountain near Yanbu in the Hijaz, proverbial for its massive presence.

3.2.4.head: هَبّود
3.2.4.meaning: Habbud, a height which al-Mubarrad distinguishes from a hollow with the similar name Habub.

4.2.2.head: وَهي
4.2.2.meaning: A fracture or weakness in what appeared to be solid stone.

4.2.5.head: الصَّيخود
4.2.5.meaning: A very hard rock, also glossed as a smooth one.

5.2.5.head: مَردود
5.2.5.meaning: An undoing or reversal that might turn an action back.

6.2.5.head: حَصيد
6.2.5.meaning: Harvested grain already cut down, set beside the stalks still standing.

7.1.4.head: مُخِبّ
7.1.4.meaning: Riders pressing their camels into a quick gait. The plural ending crosses the break.

7.2.3-4.head: مَنهَل مَورود
7.2.3-4.meaning: “A watering place all must visit”, a regular stop for travellers transferred to the encounter with death.

8.1.5.head: سوراء
8.1.5.meaning: Sura, an Iraqi locality associated with the fortress. The last sound of its name opens the second half.

8.2.4.head: المُنيف
8.2.4.meaning: High and commanding, overlooking the land around it.

8.2.5.head: المَشيد
8.2.5.meaning: Strongly built, also used of a structure finished with plaster.

9.1.3.head: بَوَّبَ
9.1.3.meaning: Furnished it with gates, whose number and material the next words specify.

10.1.2.head: جَبى
10.1.2.meaning: Is collected as tribute and brought to the ruler.

10.1.6.head: صَنعاء
10.1.6.meaning: Sana'a in Yemen. The metrical break divides its final long vowel from its closing hamza.

10.2.5.head: بَيرود
10.2.5.meaning: Bayrud, the place name in one transmission of al-Kamil. Other witnesses give Yabrud, making the geographical identification uncertain.

11.1.3.head: زَرافَة
11.1.3.meaning: Companies or troops travelling in groups.

11.2.1.head: جافِلَة
11.2.1.meaning: Surging forwards together, of horses moving at speed.

12.1.3.head: أَقصَدَ
12.1.3.meaning: Struck the target dead on the spot, as a well-aimed arrow does.

12.2.5.head: سَديد
12.2.5.meaning: Straight-flying and accurate, of an arrow that finds its mark.

13.2.3-4.head: بابا حَديد
13.2.3-4.meaning: Two iron gates, the pair fitted to the stronghold earlier in the poem.

14.1.4.head: عَمَرَ
14.1.4.meaning: Inhabited and developed the land over which they ruled.

15.1.3.head: مُعتَصِب
15.1.3.meaning: With the head bound round, the crown imagined as a headband.

15.2.3.head: الذِّمار
15.2.3.meaning: The people, covenants and sacred obligations one is honour-bound to defend.

15.2.4-5.head: جَمُّ العَديد
15.2.4-5.meaning: “Abundant in number”, attended by a great body of followers.

16.2.3-4.head: عَبد المَجيد
16.2.3-4.meaning: Abd al-Majid ibn Abd al-Wahhab al-Thaqafi, the poet's young Basran friend. Al-Mubarrad puts his age at death at about twenty.

16.2.1.head: عَلاء
16.2.1.meaning: For eminence or nobility, the quality he wishes could earn immunity from death.

17.2.2.head: رُكن
17.2.2.meaning: A load-bearing support, hence a person on whom others depend.

18.1.3.head: نَعش
18.1.3.meaning: A bier carrying the dead, distinct from the bearers underneath it.

18.2.5.head: عَفاف
18.2.5.meaning: Integrity and self-restraint, what the bearers carry without being able to weigh it.

19.1.3.head: الصَّعيد
19.1.3.meaning: The earth's surface or its soil, here what receives the body.

19.2.1.head: لِزاز
19.2.1.meaning: A close match for a rival, one who will stand his ground in a dispute.

20.1.3.head: حَثا
20.1.3.meaning: Scooped up and scattered earth by hand over the buried person.

21.2.3.head: باءَ
21.2.3.meaning: Return or resort to a place where one can find shelter.

22.1.4.head: فاضَ
22.1.4.meaning: Flow out or expire, of a soul pictured as fluid leaving its vessel.

22.2.4.head: رَبطة
22.2.4.meaning: A tied bundle, here the wrapping around the dead man. Abd al-Aziz Ibrahim prints rabta. Ibn Aqil quotes rayta, a sheet woven in one piece.

22.2.5.head: بُرد
22.2.5.meaning: Striped or figured cloths used as outer wrappings.

23.1.3-4.head: تَأمور النَّفس
23.1.3-4.meaning: “The heart's lifeblood”, the inmost vital part of the speaker's being.

23.2.5.head: جُدود
23.2.5.meaning: My fortunes or portions of good luck, as distinct from one's grandfathers.

24.1.3.meaning: Became paralysed or useless, as a hand deprived of its power.

24.2.4-5.head: يَمين الجود
24.2.4-5.meaning: “The right hand of generosity”, giving made into a person who has lost the use of a limb.

25.1.2-3.head: ماء الشَّبيبَة
25.1.2-3.meaning: “The water of youth”, the vitality that waters the figure as if it were a shoot.

25.2.5.head: الأُملود
25.2.5.meaning: Supple and tender, especially of a young branch swaying without breaking.

26.1.1.head: سَما
26.1.1.meaning: Lifted or turned upwards, of the eyes drawn to the young man.

27.2.3.meaning: The soft flesh hanging towards the throat, where a lump seems to catch.

27.2.4-5.head: حَبل الوَريد
27.2.4-5.meaning: “The cord of the jugular”, the great neck vein named beside the constriction in the throat.

28.1.2.head: دَعا
28.1.2.meaning: Call out to him personally in the hope of an answer.

29.2.3.head: هَشّ
29.2.3.meaning: Quick to brighten and respond warmly to a caller.

30.1.3.head: عِصمَة
30.1.3.meaning: Protection or a place of safety against misfortune.

30.1.4.head: أَودى
30.1.4.meaning: Swept him away or brought him to destruction.

31.1.4.head: مَقام
31.1.4.meaning: Assemblies where people gather to speak or transact public affairs.

32.1.2.head: الوُدّ
32.1.2.meaning: The bond of affection to which he feels his survival does a wrong.

32.2.5.head: جَليد
32.2.5.meaning: Hardy or exceptionally enduring, spoken as a reproach to himself.

33.2.3.head: عَيرانَة
33.2.3.meaning: A sturdy, energetic she-camel, named for strength in travel.

33.2.4.head: قَيد
33.2.4.meaning: In hobbles, restraints on a mount's stride even as it is being urged forwards.

34.2.3-4.head: طارِف وَتَليد
34.2.3-4.meaning: “My new wealth and my old”, everything recently earned and everything inherited or long held.

35.1.1.head: رَغم
35.1.1.meaning: Against my wish, with the sense of a humiliation one cannot prevent.

35.2.4.head: مَلحود
35.2.4.meaning: A grave fitted with a side niche in which the body is laid.

36.2.5.head: عود
36.2.5.meaning: My branch or stem, the growing portion of the speaker's imagined tree.

37.1.1.head: أَبلَسَ
37.1.1.meaning: Reduce someone to discomfited silence, leaving no answer.

37.1.2.head: كاشِح
37.1.2.meaning: An enemy who conceals ill will within.

37.2.2.head: جَزى
37.2.2.meaning: You repay a friend with twice the affection he shows. Both the reciter and Abd al-Aziz Ibrahim omit the opening wa. Ibn al-Mu'tazz preserves the short syllable the metre requires.

38.1.4.head: رُزء
38.1.4.meaning: A grievous loss, especially the loss of someone dear.

38.2.3-5.head: رَيب دَهر كَنود
38.2.3-5.meaning: “For a thankless age's reversals”, the misfortunes against which friends once counted on him.

39.1.3.head: أَدَب
39.1.3.meaning: His accomplishments and cultivation, including learning, manners and social grace.

39.1.4.head: تَرَدّى
39.1.4.meaning: Put on a mantle, here the new garment of youth.

40.1.1-2.head: لَهف نَفسي
40.1.1-2.meaning: “My soul's regret”, an expression of anguished longing for a lost chance of seeing him.

40.2.6.head: مَردود
40.2.6.meaning: An answering word sent back to someone who calls.

41.1.6.meaning: A persistent inward burning caused by longing or grief.

41.2.4.head: مَجهود
41.2.4.meaning: The utmost limit of my strength and exertion.

42.1.2.head: مَأتَم
42.1.2.meaning: A gathering of women mourners, the plural subject of the coming lament.

42.2.4-5.head: حُرّ الخُدود
42.2.4-5.meaning: “The fair expanse of the cheeks”, the exposed smooth skin struck in mourning.

43.2.4.head: العَميد
43.2.4.meaning: Stricken or heartsick, of a heart bowed by longing.

44.1.2.head: مَطروفَة
44.1.2.meaning: Struck in the eye or troubled by a mote, so that it constantly waters.

44.2.6.head: جودي
44.2.6.meaning: Pour forth generously, an imperative to the eye to give its tears.

45.1.2.head: عَزَّ
45.1.2.meaning: Mastered or overpowered you, said to the eye when weeping takes hold.

45.2.4.head: سَجل
45.2.4.meaning: A large bucket full of water, the imagined measure for a fresh outpouring of tears.

46.2.3-4.head: اِمتِداح القَصيد
46.2.3-4.meaning: To have odes composed in his praise, the honour in life that answers to elegy after death.
